discussion_comments.comment_body: Leaving this as is. Peak memory is about the same as before: main also held every checkpoint blob as a string at once, since all the per-file `git show` calls ran concurrently under `Promise.all`, each with its own stdout buffer. The batch buffer is released right after parsing, and blobs over 50 MB are skipped before they're read. A streaming parser would add a state machine for a constant-factor saving, which doesn't seem worth the extra complexity here.

This fetches every remote head SHA before the user has confirmed anything. On repos with many branches that can download a lot of history just to list unpublished commits. Consider limiting it to the upstream/default branch or using local remote-tracking refs.

**[P2] Apply provisioning suppression to the combined loader condition.** On a new cloud send, `beginPendingResponse` sets the optimistic marker. The coordinator emits `cloud_provisioning` through the partial-message stream before the full-state acknowledgement arrives; partial messages leave `turnState` unchanged, and that acknowledgement goes through the 50 ms state-post debounce. During this handoff, `forceShow` is still true and the provisioning message has `partial: false`, so `optimisticShow` below overrides this `false` and renders “Thinking…” alongside the progress card. This contradicts the intended suppression and adds an avoidable loader insertion/removal at startup.

Gate the combined condition passed to `useDebouncedLoaderVisibility` on the provisioning tail, keeping the hook call unconditional. The added helper-only test misses this: rendering the full hook with a provisioning tail, stale idle `turnState`, and `forceShow: true` currently returns visible. Cover that combination, then verify an `api_req_started` successor can show the loader again.

Good catch, thanks. Fixed in f8d9ca206: the provisioning check now gates the combined condition passed to `useDebouncedLoaderVisibility` (`!cloudProvisioning && (optimisticShow || isWaitingForResponse || handoffToReasoningPending)`), and the hook call stays unconditional. I moved the check out of `computeIsWaitingForResponse` instead of duplicating it, so that helper matches main again.

I replaced the helper-only test with a full-hook test: a provisioning tail, a stale idle `turnState`, and `forceShow: true` keep the loader hidden, then an `api_req_started` successor shows it again. The test fails on the previous code (`expected true to be false`) and passes with the fix.

discussion_comments.comment_body: Is a 2 minute `firstChunkMs` safe for hosted reasoning models? From what I can see in `streamText` (ai 7.0.120), the first chunk and chunk timers only reset on non-empty `text-delta`, `reasoning-delta` or `tool-input-delta` parts (plus `file`/`tool-call`). So a model that thinks for a while without streaming any reasoning text gets aborted as `before_first_chunk` even though the request is fine, and high effort runs can easily sit there past 2 minutes. Maybe only apply `firstChunkMs` when `timeoutMs` is set explicitly, or give it a much longer default than the header timeout?

in practice, does this await take a while? I'm worried that a user will toggle the switch and the switch looks stuck for a second and the user tries switching back because they thinking something is broken

good call. I measured it in local runs..

An idle toggle flips in about 85ms, same as main. The switch only waits if you click it while a session is still being set up: right after another switch, right after sending a new task’s first message, or right after resuming a task from history. How long it waits is almost entirely the remote-config fetch every session start does:
- fast API: a rebuild takes about 300ms
- API delayed 1.5s: about 1.8s
- API unresponsive: the fetch waits out its 10s timeout, so a rebuild takes about 10.3s, and a toggle landing mid-rebuild sat unflipped for 6.3s in my run

I tried to play with other factors (repo size, a hundred rules, skills and workflows, long transcripts and MCP), and they barely moved it.

For comparison, those same three moments are exactly when main breaks. The switch flips instantly, but the session ends up in the other mode. A slow API makes that more likely in exactly the cases where this PR waits longer.

So **yes, the “stuck” switch is real on slow networks**. But I think the inconsistent state is the bigger problem. It’s silent, it doesn’t heal on its own (toggling back and forth didn’t help the reporter), and it costs the user real work. The stuck switch is visible, ends on its own, and is safe: clicking again just asks for the same mode, and anything sent meanwhile waits and runs in the mode you end up seeing.

For the toggle itself, we could do this as a follow-up:
1. Flip the switch immediately with a pending state (dimmed slider or a “Switching to Act…” tooltip), and flip it back with a short explanation if the switch fails. Maybe a notification only if the wait gets long, so it doesn’t nag on every slow toggle
2. Coalesce rapid toggles, so Plan then Act before the first rebuild starts only rebuilds once

wdyt?
i think a pending state seems fine. seems more resilient to a person clicking the toggle twice in quick succession messing things up. can be follow up

🟡 **performance** (medium)

In the shell-integration fallback path, `returnCurrentTerminalContents()` already calls `getLatestTerminalOutput()` internally (which awaits it and emits the fallback message). The new telemetry code immediately calls `getLatestTerminalOutput()` a second time, so the entire clipboard capture round-trip (`workbench.action.terminal.selectAll` + `copySelection` + `clearSelection` plus two clipboard read/write operations) runs twice. The same duplication was added in the no-shell-integration branch (line 229). Besides doubling the latency/side effects of every fallback, the message that is emitted to the model and the snapshot used for the success telemetry can diverge because they come from two independent captures.

**建议**: Make `returnCurrentTerminalContents` return the snapshot it already fetched (`const terminalSnapshot = await getLatestTerminalOutput()` inside it) and reuse that value for the telemetry call, or fetch the snapshot once at the call site and derive both the emitted fallback message and the success flag from that single value.
